query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a very low volume fraction of uniformly dispersed, nanosized silicon carbide (SiC) particles to the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy will improve its fracture toughness by arresting crack propagation and refining the grain structure without perturbing its field‐induced phase transformation and consequently its large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 exhibits a large caloric response under external fields but suffers from poor structural integrity and cracking during operation.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 0.5–1 vol% high-purity, nanosized SiC particles during alloy processing so they are coherently or semi-coherently distributed (especially at grain boundaries) in the matrix.
generation.conditions: The alloy will be processed under conditions similar to the baseline caloric material (applied magnetic and pressure fields and temperature ranges used for caloric performance tests) to ensure that both mechanical and caloric properties are evaluated under realistic operational regimes.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale SiC particles dispersed along grain boundaries and within the matrix serve as crack-arresting barriers and Zener pinning centers.
generation.mechanism: The inert, high-melting-point SiC nanoparticles arrest microcrack propagation and induce modest grain refinement via Zener pinning, which together enhance the mechanical integrity. Because SiC is chemically inert and used in low volume, its presence is not expected to significantly alter the lattice parameters or interfere with the field-induced phase transformation responsible for the caloric effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified alloy, the SiC-enhanced alloy should exhibit higher fracture toughness (indicated by increased compressive strength and reduced crack propagation) while maintaining similar magnetic/pressure-induced caloric entropy change and transformation temperatures (i.e. preserving the large caloric response).
generation.baseline: The original (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy without reinforcement, which provides high caloric performance but suffers from poor mechanical integrity and crack formation.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to hold under applied-field (magnetic or pressure) operations within the temperature and loading regimes originally used for the caloric performance measurements. Testing should be performed at room temperature and in the operational field strengths where the phase transformation is induced.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies (e.g., PMC10222374 and PMC8402061) have shown that ceramic reinforcements (such as Al2O3 or TiC) can improve mechanical properties via particle dispersion, it is not established whether inert, nanoscale SiC can be introduced into a caloric high-entropy alloy without altering its sensitive field-induced phase transformation. The new aspect of this proposal is applying a low-volume, nanosized ceramic (SiC) specifically to the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 system under caloric operation conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 samples: one set processed under identical conditions without any additives and one set with 0.5–1 vol% nanosized SiC uniformly incorporated during alloy synthesis. Subject both sets to identical processing (e.g., casting/forging) and post-treatment protocols to ensure similar microstructures except for the SiC dispersion.
measurements: Determine compressive and tensile strength and fracture toughness via mechanical testing (e.g., stress–strain curves, crack propagation imaging).
Characterize microstructure using SEM/EBSD/TEM to ascertain the dispersion and interface of SiC particles.
Measure the field-induced caloric response (e.g., isothermal entropy change, transformation temperatures) under applied magnetic and pressure fields.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SiC-added samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in fracture toughness (or exhibit similar cracking behavior) OR if the caloric response (transition temperature and entropy change) is adversely affected (shifted or reduced) compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This work aims to study the influence of Al2O3 in CrFeCuMnNi high-entropy alloy matrix composites (HEMCs) on their microstructure, phase changes, and mechanical and wear performances. CrFeCuMnNi-Al2O3 HEMCs were synthesized via mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot compaction (550 °C at 550 MPa), medium frequency sintering (1200 °C), and hot forging (1000 °C at 50 MPa). The XRD results demonstrate the formation of both FCC and BCC phases in the synthesized powders, which were transformed into major stable FCC and minor ordered B2-BCC phases, as confirmed by HRSEM. The microstructural variation of HRSEM-EBSD, in terms of the coloured grain map (inverse pole figures), grain size distribution, and misorientation angle, was analysed and reported. The grain size of the matrix decreased with the increase in Al2O3 particles owing to the higher structural refinement by MA and zener pinning of the incorporated Al2O3 particles. The hot-forged CrFeCuMnNi-3 vol.% Al2O3 sample exhibited an ultimate compressive strength of 1.058 GPa, which was 21% higher than that of the unreinforced HEA matrix. The compressive mechanical properties of CoCrNi/(TiC)x (x = 0, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0) composites were measured and shown in Figure 5 and Table 2. It can be seen from the figure that the introduction of the TiC ceramic phase significantly enhanced the yield strength of the composites. Compared with the yield strength of CoCrNi alloy at 108 MPa, the yield strength of samples T6, T8, and T10 increased to 883, 1102, and 1371 MPa, respectively. The increase of yield strength can be attributed to the second phase strengthening generated by TiC particles in the composites. However, the increase of TiC content led to a simultaneous decrease in the compressive strength and plasticity of the composites. Such a result is related to the microstructure change of the composites. The size of the block TiC particles that precipitated from the composites with high content of TiC addition tends to increase and connect onto pieces (Figure 3b–d), which may decrease the composite’s deformation capacity.
